name: Sango
confidence_why: Samarin's grammar (1963, published 1967), the only first-hand description of Sango stress, says stress is not phonemic and only sometimes occurs for expressive effect, falling on the first syllable when it does, and his 1967 Basic Course tells learners not to stress any syllable, so the fixed: initial syllable label taken over from Gordon 2002 and StressTyp2 (Goedemans, Heinz & van der Hulst 2015) captures the placement but overstates the type, while Jacquot 1960 treats Bangui Sango purely as a three-tone language and says nothing about stress.

tone_statements.quote: L’injonctif se distingue du réel uniquement par l'optionalité du pronom sujet de la 2e personne du singulier, mo (17d). Le virtuel est marqué par un ton haut (noté par un accent circonflexe) sur le pronom sujet ou le préfixe verbal a-. ... Réel absolu (17a) Mbï manda farânzi. ... Virtuel absolu (17g) Mbî manda farânzi (...) (17g') (...) j’apprendrais le français.
tone_statements.translation: The injunctive differs from the realis only in the optionality of the 2sg subject pronoun mo (17d). The virtual [mood] is marked by a high tone (written with a circumflex accent) on the subject pronoun or on the verbal prefix a-. ... Realis absolute (17a) Mbï manda farânzi 'I learn French' ... Virtual absolute (17g) Mbî manda farânzi '(...) I would learn French.'
tone_statements.locator: (sheet unpaginated), 'Éléments de grammaire', paragraph on modes and aspects with examples (17a), (17g); mode table 'mô /â- V' at foot
tone_statements.summary: 4-page teaching sheet. Sole tone statement: virtual mood is marked by a high tone (circumflex) on the subject pronoun or prefix a- (mbï vs mbî). No inventory; nothing on stress; 45+ tone-marked forms.

tone_statements.quote: La variété de sango la plus répandue à Bangui possède trois tons de registre et deux tons modulés (Diki-Kidiri, c.p.). [...] Tout comme en ngbandi (cf. chapitre 1, §1.2), les tons lexicaux en sango ont une fonction distinctive. Cependant, il y a une différence entre le sango et sa langue mère : le ngbandi marque à la fois certaines catégories grammaticales d’un point de vue tonal et distingue des paires minimales, tandis qu’en sango moderne, le marquage tonal des phénomènes grammaticaux a disparu. [...] La sango n’a pas d’accent lexical, ni d’accent tonal, les deux traits dont la description exige le recours au système métrique.
tone_statements.translation: The most widespread variety of Sango in Bangui has three register tones and two contour tones (Diki-Kidiri, p.c.). [...] Just as in Ngbandi, the lexical tones of Sango have a distinctive function. However, there is a difference between Sango and its mother language: Ngbandi both marks certain grammatical categories tonally and distinguishes minimal pairs, whereas in modern Sango the tonal marking of grammatical phenomena has disappeared. [...] Sango has no lexical accent, nor tonal accent, the two features whose description requires recourse to the metrical system.

tone_statements.quote: Sango is a tonal language with three level tones: high, mid and low. Contour tones are infrequent, except in French loan words. In single syllable words of French origin the pattern is high-low falling (22–23); in longer words of French origin, all but the last syllable carries a low tone. ... Final syllables of nouns most frequently bear mid-low falling tone while verbs bear high-low falling tone. ... Tone has a low functional load, functioning mainly in the lexicon.
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (high, mid, low) on syllables; contours rare, mostly French loans, written as doubled vowels; low functional load but minimal pairs exist; -ngö imposes mid tone; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Walker, James A. & William J. Samarin. 1997. Sango phonology. In Alan S. Kaye (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa (including the Caucasus), vol. 2, 861-882. Winona Lake, IN: Eisenbrauns.
tone_statements.quote: Sango has three phonemic tones: high, mid, and low. High tone will here be signaled by an acute accent on the tone-bearing vowel (á) and low tone by a grave accent (à). Mid tone will be unmarked, except on syllabic nasals ... kà 'and, then' ka 'to sell' ká 'sore' tò 'to send' to 'to draw (water)' tó 'to throw' ... In this analysis it is said that each vowel has a tone, long vowels being analyzed as a sequence of two identical vowels. Contour tones are not a feature of Pidgin Sango—that is, changes in tone occur only on long vowels ... and never in a single vowel.
tone_statements.summary: Three register tones H, M, L, one per vowel; long vowels = two vowels, so HL/HM on them are sequences, not contours; morphemic tone only incipient in urban Sango (tone transfer). Nothing on stress.

tone_statements.quote: Sango has three phonological level tones: low (L), mid (M), and high (H) (Pasch 1993, Walker & Samarin 1997, Samarin 2000). Words have a maximal tonal density. Every syllable is thus associated with at least one tone (Gussenhoven 2004). There are also numerous tonal minimal pairs in Sango, for example, sárá /HH/ 'to itch', sārā /MM/ 'scabies', and sàrà /LL/ 'a (type of ) fish' ... Sango has many different word-tone patterns ... Word-level tonal processes are few ... there are no utterance-internal intonational pitch accents. ... Another characteristic of Sango prosody is the absence of utterance-level downstep (Walker & Samarin 1997) [p. 10]

readall_conflicts: No direct conflict between opened sources, because only one was opened. The catalog's initial-stress rule (src StressTyp2) is neither supported nor contradicted by Jacquot 1960, which treats Bangui Sango purely as a three-register tone language and never uses the word 'accent'. As context only (not a listed work, but already held by the project in the same folder): Samarin's 1967 ERIC Basic Course in Sango (lesson on tone) tells learners to 'Avoid stressing one syllable more than the others' and warns that an English speaker 'will be inclined to stress the first or second syllables of polysyllabic Sango words' because he hears high tone as main stress, which sits uneasily with a fixed: initial syllable stress record for Sango; that source should be opened properly before the catalog record is changed.

audit.recode_to: no lexical/obligatory word stress (tone language; sporadic expressive stress, which when present falls on the first syllable) -- or, if the scheme has no such class, keep 'initial' but drop strict/dominant and add a caution flag 'expressive, non-obligatory (Samarin 1963:1, 28)'
audit.reasoning: Sourcing itself is solid: the deciding text is Samarin's reference grammar (1963 typescript = 1967 Mouton), held in full with a text, and both quoted passages are verbatim at p.1 and §3.30 p.28 (p.54). The risk is in the reading, not the source. Samarin files stress under Intonation, says twice that it is 'not a significant feature of the phonemic structure', 'not lexically significant', 'used expressively', and that 'it is difficult to determine why stress sometimes occurs at all'; the initial-syllable statement describes where this optional expressive prominence lands when it occurs. His 1967 Basic Course (downloaded now, ERIC ED018784) instructs learners to avoid stressing any syllable and explains that English speakers mis-hear high tone as stress; his 2013 APiCS sketch (downloaded now) describes three tone levels and never mentions stress. No mention of word stress anywhere in the chapter.

tone.quote: Sango has three phonemic tones: high, mid, and low. High tone will here be signaled by an acute accent on the tone-bearing vowel (á) and low tone by a grave accent (à). Mid tone will be unmarked, except on syllabic nasals ... kà 'and, then' ka 'to sell' ká 'sore' tò 'to send' to 'to draw (water)' tó 'to throw' ... In this analysis it is said that each vowel has a tone, long vowels being analyzed as a sequence of two identical vowels. Contour tones are not a feature of Pidgin Sango—that is, changes in tone occur only on long vowels ... and never in a single vowel.
tone.summary: Three register tones H, M, L, one per vowel; long vowels = two vowels, so HL/HM on them are sequences, not contours; morphemic tone only incipient in urban Sango (tone transfer). Nothing on stress.
